text: Okay, so I want to welcome everybody to our meeting tonight. I want to thank our broadcasting and reporting partners who broadcast our meetings and report on them. Before we get going, I want to just speak briefly to the current state of COVID-19 in our community. And I just want to reiterate some messaging that public health has. Before I do that, I want to just thank and recognize the team of the local public health and the team at the local Ontario health team that is operating our vaccination clinic at the Memorial Gardens. I want to just recognize their great work and say to them that I've received a lot of outreach from people that have been vaccinated, who have been really impressed with the process that you've established there at the Memorial Gardens and the work you're doing and how convenient it was to get through it. So I want to thank you for that good work. I think that the local team here is doing a really good job distributing the vaccinations that we do receive. And I'm glad to see that they're doing that effectively. A global public health, along with a number of their partner public health regions in Northern Ontario have partnered to promote a stop the surge messaging. We've seen a real significant increase in cases in other parts of Northern Ontario. And we have over the last week, seen some cases in Algoma and specifically Sault Ste. Marie and Algoma that have been kind of on the increase. We've seen a half a dozen cases in the last week. One of the things that it's important to recognize is that we need to really continue to stay committed to public health advice because it's going to take a while for us to get to a vaccination level that really keeps our community safe. Important to note that people that have only received one vaccine aren't fully vaccinated. And it takes a couple of weeks for that vaccine to kick in. We have Easter weekend coming and then we have the university year ending. So we'll have students traveling home from other parts of Ontario and other parts of the country. And we obviously have a March break, which is now April break, coming up where a lot of people will be looking for things to do. In the context of this increased risk and a significant concern over the variants, the COVID variants appear to be much more transmissible and have a much more deleterious effect and obviously making more people ill that receive them. They want to reiterate a few messages. One is they really want you to be mindful in physical distancing and staying two meters apart from anybody that you are not, do not reside with, is not in your own household. It's important to recognize that a lot of people may carry COVID that are asymptomatic. So they don't have any symptoms. So you keep yourself safe. If you keep a distance between you and anybody else that isn't in your household, please wear a mask when you are inside. And when you're not inside and you're outside, your risk is lower, but there is still a risk there. But external outdoor activities are certainly encouraged over indoor activities. If you have any symptoms or if anybody in your household has any symptoms, please get tested. And while you are being tested, please have everybody in the household stay home and away from other parties. And this is a really important one. Please do not engage in any non-essential travel. Avoid traveling between zones of public health unit regions, specifically regions that have higher case counts. And please discourage travel from those regions into our own region so that we can do our best to keep our community safe. So with that, please share this messaging, encourage your family and your friends to stop the surge and to follow public health advice. And hopefully we can collectively continue to work together to keep our community safe and to give our community the time it needs to be vaccinated. So Madam Clerk, with that message shared, I'd like to start the meeting.

And whereas Autism Spectrum Disorder affects more than 135,000 Ontarians and ASD is now recognized as the most common neurological disorder, affecting one in every 66 children, as well as their friends, family, and community. Whereas ASD is a spectrum disorder, which means it not only manifests itself differently in every individual in whom it appears, but its characteristics will change over the life of each individual as well. A child with ASD will become an adult with ASD. Whereas Autism Ontario, formerly Autism Society Ontario, is the leading source of information referral on autism and one of the largest collective voices representing the autism community. Since 1973, Autism Ontario has been providing support information and opportunities for thousands of families across the province. Whereas Autism Ontario is dedicated to increasing public awareness about autism and the day-to-day issues faced by individuals with autism, their families, and the professions with whom they interact. The association and its chapter share common goals of providing information, education, support, research, and advocating for programs and services for the autism community. speaker: donmcconnell
text: Certainly, through you, Mr. Mayor, to Councilor Rezo Allen, the 30% number originally came from a provincial government directive back in the mid 1990s, and it's still in our official plan. You'll see the industry use it a lot, a lot of municipalities use it. When you talk to municipal affairs staff, they frequently use it. The Ministry of Municipal Affairs and Housing does do detailed analysis of property sales in Sault Ste. Marie for every municipality in the province.
